source_text: Sic disputavi hactenus, ut mos nostrae fidei postulabat; verum non hac solum parte contentus, agam tecum benigne, et consulto eam mihi personam induam, quae praeceptoris tui sententiae favere videatur. Hoc autem ea gratia fiet, ut tu in Manichaeum, si ab eo dissides, oppugnare cogaris. Assertioni quippe nostrae nihil astutiae inesse hoc ipso docebitur, cum Traducianus non invenit, quo Manichaeo possit obsistere. Itaque apparebit quanta inter vos coniuratio sit, quam procuretis mutuis cuncta compendiis, quando inter vos iurgium excitari non potuerit. Quo igitur id me consilio arripuisse ostenderim, animo lectoris insidat; nunc iam personae, quam assumimus, oratione fungamur. Errant omnino qui putant hanc concretionem corporis habilem esse iustitiae; omnibus bonis studiis repugnat vilis natura carnis et sanguinis. Quidquid irritamentorum est lenocinio sensuum, ad perturbationem, immo eversionem mentis elabitur, quae in hoc coenum nescio qua infelicitate deiecta, generosos micatus luteo perdit admixtu. Ipsa quantum in se est ad locum suum, id est, ad superiora conatur; sed terreno afflictatur ergastulo. Denique cum ad pudicitiam voluerit subvolare, gluten et viscum voluptatis obscenae de perustis visceribus experitur. Iam si liberalitatem munificentiae concupiscat, avaritiae, quae tegmine frugalitatis operitur, manicis arctissimis colligatur. Enim vero si in aequabili constantiae quadam voluerit serenitate consistere, obruitur illico grandine timoris, et doloris procellis, atque ad omnia exsanguescens dubia, compos sui non sinitur manere consilii. Iunge huc ignoratarum rerum noctem, qua circumdatur illuvie. Quid laudabilitatis in eo suspicabimur animante, qui nec ad utilium electionem oculos vigentes habet, et inter tempestates cupiditatum et discriminum sua naufragia numerare non sufficit? Nec tamen aliquis haec sponte depravatae substantiae accidisse mentiatur; ipsa primorum hominum institutio his aerumnis invenitur obnoxia. Nam ut hoc etiam Moysi, quem Catholici venerantur, testimonio comprobetur, experiebantur primi homines carnificinam timoris, quos intentatio, nisi obedissent, periculi territabat, quantumque de rerum collatione metiendum est, formidolosiores posteris eos opinamur fuisse, quos poena necdum cuiquam comperta vexabat. Cur enim mortis intentatione quaterentur, qui nesciebant quid incommodi afferret interitus? Sollicitabantur nimirum solis suspicionibus malorum. In qua ergo ille animus tranquillitate consisteret, quem tam aspera hiems formidinis commovebat? Porro ignorantia quam profunda, quamque patiendi eius dura conditio, ut liberari ab ea nisi praevaricatione non posset; scientiam quippe boni malique, absque ausu condemnabili nequaquam capessiturus. Hoc ita caecum et aerumnosum animal, inquies etiam cupiditas innata reddebat, quam rei interdictae et venustas irritabat et suavitas. Quod totum velut parum esset ad infelicitatem illius exprimendam, impugnationi naturae superioris exponitur. Quis ergo adeo desipiat, ut ibi quidquam boni fuisse arbitretur, ubi tot miseriarum instrumenta instituta fateatur? Pessimae igitur conditionis, pessimaeque naturae caro ista in istis primis hominibus suum, quod ab exordio tenebat, exseruit. Hanc autem tam malam substantiam Deus bonus non potuit fabricare. Quid ergo superest, nisi ut fateamur alterum esse animae datorem, alterum luteorum conditorem? Stat certe Manichaei, cuius indueram personam, acies ordinata. Quid opperiamur intellegis, videlicet ut qui ei adversus est, consequenti impugnatione id demonstret. Igitur vestrum dogma cum eo confligat; apparebit utrum sine pernicie sua vel leviter possit moveri. Pronuntiavit certe, non solum nasci omnes de commixtione corporum criminosos, verum ipsum Adam culparum necessitatem de concretione viscerum, et limi ex quo factus est sordibus attulisse. Natura, inquit, carnis in primis hominibus fuit noxia; ipsam scintillam animi studio honestatis sublucentem conclusit, madefecit, exstinxit. Ineptiunt prorsus Catholici, qui peccantium testimoniis obnituntur, et nec documentis propriis acquiescunt, videntesque non se bonum quod volunt agere, sed malum quod exsecrantur operari, putant tamen in carne non esse mali necessitatem. His ergo tam invidiose dictis congrediatur Traducianus, si potest; ego interim spectator assisto, et exitum vestri conflictus opperior. Quid itaque respondebis malam naturam etiam in primis hominibus fuisse iuranti? Sine dubio referes Deum formatorem hominum non potuisse malum condere quod creavit, et ideo quia Deus qui malum non facit, homines fecit, nequaquam eos naturaliter malos probari. Dixisti aliquid, et veraciter: sed vide utrum hoc me debueris audiente proferre. Qua enim virtute Manichaeum concusseris non satis curo; interim in mea totus iura transisti. Capto tibi iam delectat illudere; excipio quippe magno plausu professionem tuam, teque ut eius memineris admoneo. Dignitate enim auctoris, id est Dei, qui malum non facit, pronuntiasti opera eius bona debere asseri. Omnes ergo homines de instituta a Deo sexuum commixtione generatos, a Deo, an a diabolo fieri putas? Si a Deo: qui eos audes reos malosque pronuntiare, cum unicum dixeris esse testimonium Adam fieri malae non potuisse naturae, quia conditus a Deo qui est optimus, indicetur? Si ergo argumentum forte est, per quod credatur primorum hominum rea non instituta substantia, hoc ipsum quia Deus eam condidit quem bonum fatemur; remanet illud in excidium traducis, ut et omnes de coniugio genitos iniquos condi non posse, eodem testimonio comprobetur, quia Deus eos condidit, quem bonum fatemur. Sin autem et post hoc rabiens impudentia iurare perstiterit, et a Deo fieri parvulos, et tamen malos esse eos naturaliter; catholico quidem, sicut et Deo nostro, nihil his mendaciis praeiudicii comparatur; Manichaeum tamen constat a vobis oppugnatum non esse, qui libenter quod Deum criminaris amplectitur; illud tibi perisse contentus, per quod Adam conditionis bonae fueras approbare molitus.
pass_a_gloss: I have disputed thus far as the custom of our faith was demanding; but not content with this part alone, I will treat with you kindly, and by design I will put on myself that person which may seem to favor your teacher's sentence. But this will be done for this grace, that you may be compelled to attack into Manichaeus, if you dissent from him. For it will be taught by this itself that no cunning is in our assertion, when the Traducian does not find by which he can resist Manichaeus. And thus it will appear how great a conspiracy there is between you, how you procure all things by mutual shortcuts, when a quarrel cannot be stirred between you. Therefore that I may have shown with what counsel I snatched this, let it sit in the reader's mind; now already let us perform by the speech of the person which we assume. They altogether err who think this concretion of the body is fit for justice; the cheap nature of flesh and blood fights against all good studies. Whatever of irritants there is by the pimping of the senses slides toward a disturbance, nay an overturning of the mind, which thrown down I know not by what unhappiness into this filth loses generous sparkles by a muddy mixture. It itself as much as is in it tries toward its own place, that is toward the higher; but it is afflicted by an earthly prison. Finally when it has wanted to fly up to modesty, it experiences the glue and birdlime of obscene pleasure from burned viscera. Now if it desires the liberality of munificence, it is bound by the tightest manacles of avarice, which is covered by a covering of frugality. For indeed if it has wanted to stand in a certain equal serenity of constancy, it is immediately overwhelmed by a hail of fear, and by storms of pain, and growing bloodless toward all doubtful things, it is not allowed to remain possessor of its own counsel. Join hither the night of unknown things, by which it is surrounded with filth. What of praiseworthiness will we suspect in that living being, who neither has thriving eyes for the choice of useful things, and among the storms of desires and of discriminations does not suffice to number his own shipwrecks? Nor nevertheless let anyone lie that these things happened by the will of a depraved substance; the very institution of the first humans is found liable to these hardships. For that this also may be proved by the testimony of Moses, whom the Catholics venerate, the first humans were experiencing the butchery of fear, whom the threat of danger, unless they had obeyed, was terrifying, and as far as it must be measured from a comparison of things, we opine they were more fearful than posterity, whom a penalty not yet found by anyone was vexing. For why would they be shaken by a threat of death, who did not know what inconvenience destruction would bring? They were solicited indeed by suspicions of evils alone. In what tranquillity therefore would that mind stand, which so harsh a winter of fear was moving? Further ignorance how deep, and how hard a condition of suffering it, that he could not be freed from it except by prevarication; for he was by no means about to take knowledge of good and evil without a condemnable daring. This animal so blind and hardship-full, an inborn desire also even restless was rendering, which both the charm and the sweetness of a forbidden thing was irritating. Which whole as if it were too little for expressing his unhappiness, he is exposed to the attack of a higher nature. Who therefore would so be foolish, that he would judge anything of good had been there, where he would confess so many instruments of miseries instituted? Of a worst condition therefore, and of a worst nature, this flesh in those first humans put forth its own, which it was holding from the beginning. But a good God could not fabricate so evil a substance. What therefore remains, except that we confess one is the giver of the soul, another the founder of muddy things? The battle-line of Manichaeus, whose person I had put on, certainly stands ordered. You understand what we wait, namely that he who is against him may show that by a consequent attack. Therefore let your dogma conflict with him; it will appear whether it can even lightly be moved without its own destruction. He pronounced certainly not only that all are born criminal from the mingling of bodies, but that Adam himself brought a necessity of faults from the concretion of viscera, and from the filths of the mud from which he was made. The nature, he says, of flesh in the first humans was harmful; it enclosed, soaked, extinguished that spark of the mind faintly shining by a zeal of honorableness. The Catholics are altogether inept, who resist by testimonies of those sinning, and do not even acquiesce in their own documents, and seeing that they do not do the good which they will, but work the evil which they execrate, nevertheless think there is not a necessity of evil in the flesh. Let the Traducian therefore join battle with these things so invidiously said, if he can; I meanwhile stand as spectator, and wait the end of your conflict. What therefore will you reply to him swearing that an evil nature was even in the first humans? Without doubt you will report that God the former of humans could not found the evil which he created, and therefore because God who does not make evil made humans, they are by no means proved naturally evil. You said something, and truly: but see whether you ought to have brought this forth with me hearing. For by what virtue you shall have shaken Manichaeus I do not much care; meanwhile you have altogether crossed into my rights. It now delights to mock you caught; for I receive your profession with great applause, and I advise you that you remember it. For by the dignity of the author, that is of God, who does not make evil, you pronounced that his works ought to be asserted good. All humans therefore generated from a mingling of the sexes instituted by God, do you think them made by God, or by the devil? If by God: you who dare to pronounce them guilty and evil, when you shall have said there is a unique testimony that Adam could not have been made of an evil nature, because he is indicated founded by God who is best? If therefore the argument is strong, through which it is believed that the substance of the first humans was not instituted guilty, this itself because God founded it whom we confess good; that remains into the destruction of the tradux, that even all generated from marriage cannot be founded unjust, is proved by the same testimony, because God founded them, whom we confess good. But if even after this raging shamelessness shall have persisted to swear, both that little ones are made by God, and nevertheless that they are evil naturally; for the catholic indeed, as also for our God, no prior judgment is furnished by these lies; yet it stands that Manichaeus was not attacked by you, who freely embraces that you accuse God; content that that has perished for you, through which you had been trying to approve Adam of a good condition.

pass_b_english: So far I have argued as the practice of our faith required. But I will not be content with this approach alone. I shall deal generously with you and deliberately take on a role that seems to favor your teacher’s position. The purpose is to force you to attack Mani, if you disagree with him. The absence of trickery in our argument will be shown by the very fact that the advocate of inherited sin can find no way to oppose Mani. Thus the extent of your conspiracy and the mutual advantages by which you manage everything will appear when no quarrel can be stirred up between you. Let the reader keep in mind the purpose I have explained for taking this course. Now let us speak in the role we assume.

[Julian argues in an assumed Manichaean voice:] ‘Those who think this bodily formation capable of justice are completely mistaken. The lowly nature of flesh and blood opposes every good pursuit. Every stimulus, through the seduction of the senses, slides into disturbing—indeed overthrowing—the mind. Cast into this mire by some unknown misfortune, the mind loses its noble flashes of light through mixture with clay. Of itself it strives toward its own place, toward the heights, but it is crushed in an earthly prison. When it wishes to fly upward to chastity, it encounters the glue and birdlime of obscene pleasure rising from burning inward parts.

‘If it desires generous liberality, it is bound in the tightest shackles of greed, disguised as thrift. If it wishes to stand in a balanced serenity of steadfastness, it is immediately overwhelmed by a hailstorm of fear and tempests of pain. Turning bloodless before every uncertainty, it cannot remain master of its own judgment. Add the night of ignorance, whose filth surrounds it. What praiseworthy quality shall we suppose in a living being that has neither keen eyes to choose useful things nor the ability to count its shipwrecks among the storms of desires and dangers?

‘Let no one falsely claim these things happened to a substance voluntarily corrupted. The original making of the first humans is found subject to these miseries. To prove this even from Moses, whom catholics revere: the first humans experienced fear’s torture, terrified by the threat of danger unless they obeyed. So far as comparison allows us to judge, we think them more fearful than their descendants, since a punishment as yet experienced by no one tormented them. Why should the threat of death shake people who did not know what harm death would bring? Mere suspicions of evils plainly troubled them. In what tranquility could a mind stand when such a bitter winter of fear disturbed it?

‘And how profound its ignorance, how harsh the condition of enduring it, when it could be freed only by transgression! It would obtain knowledge of good and evil only through an act of condemnable daring. This living being, already so blind and miserable, was made restless too by inborn desire, provoked by the beauty and sweetness of the forbidden thing. As though all this were too little to express its unhappiness, it was exposed to attack by a higher nature. Who, then, could be foolish enough to suppose any good existed where he acknowledges so many instruments of misery were established?

‘This flesh, then, of the worst condition and worst nature, displayed in those first humans what it had possessed from the beginning. The good God could not have made so evil a substance. What remains except to acknowledge one giver of the soul and another creator of creatures of clay?’

Mani’s battle line, whose role I had adopted, now stands in formation. You understand what we await: whoever opposes him must demonstrate it through a consistent attack. Let your doctrine fight him, then; it will appear whether it can make even a slight movement without destroying itself. He has certainly pronounced not only that everyone born from bodily union is criminal, but that Adam himself brought the necessity of faults from the formation of his inward parts and from the dirt of the clay from which he was made. He says: ‘Flesh’s nature was harmful in the first humans. It shut in, drenched, and extinguished the very spark of mind that glimmered with the pursuit of honor. Catholics are utterly foolish: they resist sinners’ testimony and will not accept even their own evidence. They see themselves not doing the good they want but performing the evil they detest (Romans 7:19), yet think there is no necessity of evil in the flesh.’

Let the advocate of inherited sin meet these highly prejudicial claims, if he can. For now I stand as a spectator and await the outcome of your conflict. What will you answer someone swearing that nature was evil even in the first humans? Undoubtedly you will reply that God, humanity’s maker, could not create evil in what he made. Therefore, since God, who does no evil, made humans, they cannot be proved naturally evil. You have said something, and truly. But consider whether you should have said it within my hearing. I care little how forcefully you shook Mani; meanwhile you have passed entirely into my jurisdiction.

Now that you are captured, I enjoy teasing you. I greet your profession with great applause and remind you to remember it. From the dignity of its author—that is, God, who does no evil—you pronounced that his works must be affirmed good. Do you think, then, that all humans generated by the sexual union God established are made by God or by the devil? If by God, how dare you pronounce them guilty and evil, when you said the decisive proof that Adam could not have been made with an evil nature was that he was created by God, who is perfectly good?

If this is a strong argument for believing the first humans’ substance was not established guilty—precisely that God, whom we acknowledge good, created it—then the same argument remains to destroy inherited sin. It proves that everyone born from marriage cannot be created unjust, because God, whom we acknowledge good, creates them. But if, even after this, raging shamelessness persists in swearing both that infants are made by God and that they are naturally evil, these lies bring no prejudice against a catholic or our God. Yet plainly you have not attacked Mani. He gladly embraces your accusation against God, content that you have lost the argument through which you tried to establish Adam’s good condition.

choices.why: Julian's polemic target is inherited sin as a natural evil (malum naturale), the vine-layer metaphor, not a later systematic 'original sin' slogan and not soul-traducianism as such.
rejected: original sin (later system as default gloss)
traducianism of the soul (not the load here)

choices.why: Julian defends marriage as God's work against the charge that generation transmits sin.
Julian's Manichaean charge: an evil that is a nature, not a will's act.
